# Consortium Profile: Secure Food Robotics Initiative

This document outlines the core partners committed to the joint development of resilient AI decision support and robotic automation for food logistics. The consortium brings together expertise in computer security, robotics, food microbiology, and systems engineering. As of 10 September 2026, the Fictional German university coordinator (TUF), independent Italian robotics SME (ALV), Spanish food microbiology institute (IMAA) and Austrian logistics cooperative (AKK) have signed participation agreements for the upcoming proposal.

## Coordinator: Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF), Germany

**Role:** Project coordination, systems engineering, and computer security.

The Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF) is a leading research institution in Germany, hosting the Secure Cyber-Physical Systems Group led by Prof. Dr. Lukas Varnkötter. TUF will oversee the integration of security protocols and resilient AI decision-support systems. The group has extensive experience in designing algorithms that detect and mitigate sensor faults and adversarial data injections in distributed networks. TUF will ensure that the data pipelines connecting robotic platforms, environmental sensors, and decision engines remain secure and reliable under operational stress.

## Partner 1: Automazione Logistica Veloce S.r.l. (ALV), Italy

**Role:** Robotic hardware provision, autonomous navigation, and mechatronics.

ALV is an independent Italian robotics SME based in Turin, specialising in the design and deployment of Autonomous Guided Vehicles (AGVs) for industrial warehousing. Founded in 2015, ALV has a strong track record of developing agile robotic solutions for dynamic environments. Within the consortium, ALV is responsible for the physical robotic platforms and the low-level control systems. Their engineering team will implement the fault-tolerant navigation algorithms developed by TUF onto the robotic hardware, ensuring that the AGVs can safely operate even when individual sensors degrade or fail.

## Partner 2: Instituto de Microbiología Alimentaria de Aragón (IMAA), Spain

**Role:** Food microbiology, spoilage modelling, and hazard assessment.

IMAA is a Spanish public research institute located in Zaragoza, dedicated to advancing food safety and quality. The institute brings critical domain expertise in food microbiology to the consortium. IMAA will develop predictive models for microbial growth and spoilage under varying environmental conditions, specifically focusing on interrupted cold chains. Cold-chain adaptation can combine the Spanish laboratory and Austrian operator to create a comprehensive farm-to-fork validation pipeline. IMAA's researchers will define the biological constraints and safety thresholds that the AI decision-support system must respect when optimising logistics operations.

## Partner 3: Alpen-Kühlkette eG (AKK), Austria

**Role:** Logistics operations, cold-chain infrastructure, and end-user validation.

Alpen-Kühlkette eG (AKK) is an Austrian logistics cooperative headquartered in Innsbruck, operating a network of temperature-controlled warehouses and distribution centres across Central Europe. AKK represents the end-user perspective, providing the operational context and infrastructure necessary for testing and validating the consortium's technologies. They will supply historical environmental data, define operational requirements, and facilitate the deployment of prototype systems within their facilities to ensure that the developed solutions meet the rigorous demands of commercial food logistics.

## Informal Contact: University of Boreal Sciences, Canada

**Role:** Advisory on North American logistics standards.

Dr. Elias Thorne, a researcher at the University of Boreal Sciences in Canada, serves as an informal contact for the consortium. His research focuses on trans-Atlantic supply chain interoperability. He provides ad-hoc advice on North American regulatory frameworks and logistics standards. Because he is an informal contact and not a participating beneficiary, he does not count as an EU/associated-country entity for the stated minimum participation requirements, despite Canada's association to Horizon Europe Pillar II. His involvement is strictly advisory and involves no transfer of funds or formal contractual obligations.

# Final Report: RESIL-BOT (2022–2025)

**Resilient Anomaly Detection for Autonomous Guided Vehicles in Warehousing**

**Funding Agency:** German Research Foundation (DFG)
**Grant Number:** RB-2022-8849-TUF
**Total Budget:** EUR 1,200,000
**Duration:** 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025
**Principal Investigator:** Prof. Dr. Lukas Varnkötter, Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF)

## 1. Executive Summary

The RESIL-BOT project aimed to enhance the operational resilience of Autonomous Guided Vehicles (AGVs) in warehouse environments by developing advanced anomaly detection algorithms. The primary focus was on identifying sensor faults and adversarial data injections to provide a foundation for bounded operational safety. Over the four-year period, the project successfully developed a novel AI-driven decision-support framework capable of isolating faulty sensor streams in replay evaluations.

## 2. Objectives

1.  Characterise the statistical properties of common sensor faults (e.g., drift, noise, complete failure) in LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors used on warehouse AGVs.
2.  Develop a lightweight, real-time anomaly detection engine capable of running on edge hardware.
3.  Evaluate the detection accuracy and false-positive rate of the engine using historical and synthetic sensor traces.
4.  Design fallback navigation policies that allow AGVs to safely halt or return to base when critical sensor thresholds are breached.

## 3. Methodology

The project utilised a data-driven approach, collecting over 4,500 hours of baseline sensor data from AGVs operating in controlled environments. We injected synthetic faults into these data streams to create a comprehensive testing corpus. The anomaly detection engine was built using a semi-supervised learning architecture, trained exclusively on 3,300 hours of healthy data, with the remaining 1,200 hours used for validation. The 80 test traces used for final evaluation were strictly separated from training and validation sets.

To evaluate the system, we constructed a replay testing framework. This allowed us to feed the recorded and modified sensor traces into the detection engine in real-time, mimicking the data flow of a live AGV without the physical risks associated with testing faulty navigation in a populated warehouse.

## 4. Key Results and Performance Metrics

*   **Fault Detection Accuracy:** In 2025, we completed replay tests on 80 independent sensor traces (each containing exactly one injected fault). The system detected 68 of the 80 injected faults (85 percent, Wilson 95% CI approximately 76 to 91 percent). 
*   **False Positive Rate:** The engine was evaluated over 1,200 hours of healthy validation data, partitioned into 72,000 one-minute decision windows. It flagged 1,728 of these windows as anomalous, resulting in a false positive rate of 2.4%. The operational disruption this would cause in a live setting remains to be measured.
*   **Latency:** The edge-optimised detection algorithm achieved an average inference time of 14 milliseconds (SD = 2.1 ms, n = 10,000 inferences) on a standard ARM Cortex-A76 edge node, well within the 50-millisecond requirement for real-time AGV control loops.
*   **Limitation Note:** While the detection metrics are highly promising, it is critical to acknowledge the boundaries of the current validation. These were simulations, not live warehouse validations. The replay tests demonstrated the detector's performance, but closed-loop navigation safety and operational disruption remain to be validated in live settings.

## 5. Dissemination and Open Data

The project resulted in four peer-reviewed publications in top-tier security and robotics venues. Furthermore, we have released the "RESIL-BOT Warehouse Sensor Corpus," an open dataset containing 2.5 TB of annotated LiDAR, ultrasonic, and IMU data, published under a CC BY 4.0 license to support further research in the community.

# Consortium Resources and Infrastructure

This document details the physical infrastructure, hardware, and laboratory facilities available to the consortium partners as of September 2026.

## 1. Robotics Hardware (Automazione Logistica Veloce S.r.l.)

ALV maintains a dedicated 800-square-meter mechatronics testing facility in Turin. The facility is equipped with motion capture systems for precise ground-truth tracking of robotic platforms. 

Regarding the robotic fleet available for research and development: A planned 30-device robot fleet has zero units acquired at present, as procurement is contingent on future capital expenditure approvals. However, six existing bench robots suffice for an initial bounded study. These bench robots are fully functional, scaled-down AGV prototypes equipped with the complete sensor suite (LiDAR, ultrasonic, RGB-D cameras) and compute modules intended for the final production models. They are ideal for validating navigation algorithms, fault-tolerance mechanisms, and edge-computing workloads in a controlled environment before scaling up to full-size industrial vehicles.

## 2. Food Microbiology Laboratory (Instituto de Microbiología Alimentaria de Aragón)

IMAA operates a state-of-the-art 400-square-meter BSL-2 laboratory in Zaragoza. The facility includes:

*   Four walk-in environmental chambers capable of simulating complex temperature and humidity profiles, essential for replicating interrupted cold chains.
*   High-throughput sequencing equipment for rapid microbial profiling.
*   Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for detecting volatile spoilage markers.

The lab can assay food samples to quantify microbial load, identify pathogens, and measure biochemical degradation over time. 

**Important Regulatory Note:** No medicinal-product development expertise or approval exists within IMAA or the broader consortium. The institute's mandate and certifications are strictly limited to food safety, agricultural research, and environmental monitoring. The team does not conduct pharmacological research, nor do they develop human or veterinary medicines.

## 3. Logistics Infrastructure (Alpen-Kühlkette eG)

AKK provides access to its primary distribution centre in Innsbruck, Austria. The facility spans 12,000 square meters and features three distinct temperature zones: ambient (15°C to 25°C), chilled (2°C to 8°C), and frozen (-25°C to -18°C). The warehouse is equipped with a dense network of IoT environmental sensors logging temperature and humidity at 5-minute intervals.

**Operational Update:**
Per an operator notice dated 21 September 2026, AKK management withdraws access to live refrigeration control interfaces for all external research projects due to updated internal risk management policies. Read-only monitoring remains authorised, allowing the consortium to continuously ingest real-time environmental data from the warehouse sensor network. Furthermore, an isolated thermal bench is available at the Innsbruck site; this standalone unit is physically decoupled from the main commercial storage areas and can be used for experimental manipulation of temperature profiles without risking commercial inventory.

Because live control of the commercial warehouse environment is no longer permitted, full validation of changed operating policies must be planned with access gates. Any proposed changes to AGV routing, door management, or cooling schedules generated by the AI decision-support system must pass through a human-in-the-loop verification step and be tested on the isolated thermal bench or via simulation before being considered for operational deployment.

# Final Report: RESIL-BOT (2022–2025)

**Resilient Anomaly Detection for Autonomous Guided Vehicles in Warehousing**

**Funding Agency:** German Research Foundation (DFG)
**Grant Number:** RB-2022-8849-TUF
**Total Budget:** EUR 1,200,000
**Duration:** 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025
**Principal Investigator:** Prof. Dr. Lukas Reuter, Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF)

## 1. Executive Summary

The RESIL-BOT project aimed to enhance the operational resilience of Autonomous Guided Vehicles (AGVs) in warehouse environments by developing advanced anomaly detection algorithms. The primary focus was on identifying and mitigating sensor faults and adversarial data injections that could compromise navigation and safety. Over the four-year period, the project successfully developed a novel AI-driven decision-support framework capable of isolating faulty sensor streams and maintaining bounded operational safety.

## 2. Objectives

1.  Characterise the statistical properties of common sensor faults (e.g., drift, noise, complete failure) in LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors used on warehouse AGVs.
2.  Develop a lightweight, real-time anomaly detection engine capable of running on edge hardware.
3.  Evaluate the detection accuracy and false-positive rate of the engine using historical and synthetic sensor traces.
4.  Design fallback navigation policies that allow AGVs to safely halt or return to base when critical sensor thresholds are breached.

## 3. Methodology

The project utilised a data-driven approach, collecting over 4,500 hours of baseline sensor data from AGVs operating in controlled environments. We injected synthetic faults into these data streams to create a comprehensive testing corpus. The anomaly detection engine was built using a semi-supervised learning architecture, trained exclusively on healthy data to identify deviations indicative of faults or attacks.

To evaluate the system, we constructed a replay testing framework. This allowed us to feed the recorded and modified sensor traces into the detection engine in real-time, mimicking the data flow of a live AGV without the physical risks associated with testing faulty navigation in a populated warehouse.

## 4. Key Results and Performance Metrics

*   **Fault Detection Accuracy:** In the final evaluation phase, we completed 2025 replay tests on 80 sensor traces. The system detected 68 injected faults (85 percent, Wilson 95% CI approximately 76 to 91 percent). 
*   **False Positive Rate:** The engine maintained a false positive rate of 2.4% across 1,200 hours of healthy validation data, ensuring that operational disruptions due to false alarms were minimised.
*   **Latency:** The edge-optimised detection algorithm achieved an average inference time of 14 milliseconds on standard ARM Cortex-A processors, well within the 50-millisecond requirement for real-time AGV control loops.
*   **Limitation Note:** While the detection metrics are highly promising, it is critical to acknowledge the boundaries of the current validation. These were simulations, not live warehouse validations. The replay tests relied on pre-recorded traces, and the system has not yet been subjected to the unpredictable dynamics of a fully operational, human-populated logistics centre.

## 5. Dissemination and Open Data

The project resulted in four peer-reviewed publications in top-tier security and robotics venues. Furthermore, we have released the "RESIL-BOT Warehouse Sensor Corpus," an open dataset containing 2.5 TB of annotated LiDAR, ultrasonic, and IMU data, published under a CC BY 4.0 license to support further research in the community.

**Funding Agency:** German Research Foundation (DFG)
**Grant Number:** RB-2022-8849-TUF
**Total Budget:** EUR 1,200,000
**Duration:** 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2025
**Principal Investigator:** Prof. Dr. Lukas Reuter, Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF)

## 1. Executive Summary

The RESIL-BOT project aimed to enhance the operational resilience of Autonomous Guided Vehicles (AGVs) in warehouse environments by developing advanced anomaly detection algorithms. The primary focus was on identifying sensor faults and adversarial data injections to provide a foundation for bounded operational safety. Over the four-year period, the project successfully developed a novel AI-driven decision-support framework capable of isolating faulty sensor streams in replay evaluations.

## 2. Objectives

1.  Characterise the statistical properties of common sensor faults (e.g., drift, noise, complete failure) in LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors used on warehouse AGVs.
2.  Develop a lightweight, real-time anomaly detection engine capable of running on edge hardware.
3.  Evaluate the detection accuracy and false-positive rate of the engine using historical and synthetic sensor traces.
4.  Design fallback navigation policies that allow AGVs to safely halt or return to base when critical sensor thresholds are breached.

## 3. Methodology

The project utilised a data-driven approach, collecting over 4,500 hours of baseline sensor data from AGVs operating in controlled environments. We injected synthetic faults into these data streams to create a comprehensive testing corpus. The anomaly detection engine was built using a semi-supervised learning architecture, trained exclusively on 3,300 hours of healthy data, with the remaining 1,200 hours used for validation. *   **Fault Detection Accuracy:** In 2025, we completed replay tests on 80 independent sensor traces (each containing exactly one injected fault). The system detected 68 of the 80 injected faults (85 percent, Wilson 95% CI approximately 76 to 91 percent). 
*   **False Positive Rate:** The engine was evaluated over 1,200 hours of healthy validation data, partitioned into 72,000 one-minute decision windows. The project resulted in four peer-reviewed publications in top-tier security and robotics venues. My research bridges computer security and systems engineering, with a specific focus on the resilience of cyber-physical systems (CPS) in logistics and robotics. # Consortium Profile: Secure Food Robotics Initiative

This document outlines the core partners committed to the joint development of resilient AI decision support and robotic automation for food logistics. The consortium brings together expertise in computer security, robotics, food microbiology, and systems engineering. As of 10 September 2026, the Fictional German university coordinator (TUF), independent Italian robotics SME (ALV), Spanish food microbiology institute (IMAA) and Austrian logistics cooperative (AKK) have signed participation agreements for the upcoming proposal.

## Coordinator: Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF), Germany

**Role:** Project coordination, systems engineering, and computer security.

The Technical University of Falkenburg (TUF) is a leading research institution in Germany, hosting the Secure Cyber-Physical Systems Group led by Prof. Dr. Lukas Reuter. TUF will oversee the integration of security protocols and resilient AI decision-support systems. The group has extensive experience in designing algorithms that detect and mitigate sensor faults and adversarial data injections in distributed networks. TUF will ensure that the data pipelines connecting robotic platforms, environmental sensors, and decision engines remain secure and reliable under operational stress.

## Partner 1: Automazione Logistica Veloce S.r.l. (ALV), Italy

**Role:** Robotic hardware provision, autonomous navigation, and mechatronics.

ALV is an independent Italian robotics SME based in Turin, specialising in the design and deployment of Autonomous Guided Vehicles (AGVs) for industrial warehousing. Founded in 2015, ALV has a strong track record of developing agile robotic solutions for dynamic environments. Within the consortium, ALV is responsible for the physical robotic platforms and the low-level control systems. Their engineering team will implement the fault-tolerant navigation algorithms developed by TUF onto the robotic hardware, ensuring that the AGVs can safely operate even when individual sensors degrade or fail.

## Partner 2: Instituto de Microbiología Alimentaria de Aragón (IMAA), Spain

**Role:** Food microbiology, spoilage modelling, and hazard assessment.

IMAA is a Spanish public research institute located in Zaragoza, dedicated to advancing food safety and quality. The institute brings critical domain expertise in food microbiology to the consortium. IMAA will develop predictive models for microbial growth and spoilage under varying environmental conditions, specifically focusing on interrupted cold chains. Cold-chain adaptation can combine the Spanish laboratory and Austrian operator to create a comprehensive farm-to-fork validation pipeline. IMAA's researchers will define the biological constraints and safety thresholds that the AI decision-support system must respect when optimising logistics operations.

## Partner 3: Alpen-Kühlkette eG (AKK), Austria

**Role:** Logistics operations, cold-chain infrastructure, and end-user validation.

Alpen-Kühlkette eG (AKK) is an Austrian logistics cooperative headquartered in Innsbruck, operating a network of temperature-controlled warehouses and distribution centres across Central Europe. AKK represents the end-user perspective, providing the operational context and infrastructure necessary for testing and validating the consortium's technologies. They will supply historical environmental data, define operational requirements, and facilitate the deployment of prototype systems within their facilities to ensure that the developed solutions meet the rigorous demands of commercial food logistics.

## Informal Contact: University of Boreal Sciences, Canada

**Role:** Advisory on North American logistics standards.

Dr. Elias Thorne, a researcher at the University of Boreal Sciences in Canada, serves as an informal contact for the consortium. His research focuses on trans-Atlantic supply chain interoperability. He provides ad-hoc advice on North American regulatory frameworks and logistics standards. Because he is an informal contact and not a participating beneficiary, he does not count as an EU/associated-country entity for the stated minimum participation requirements, despite Canada's association to Horizon Europe Pillar II. His involvement is strictly advisory and involves no transfer of funds or formal contractual obligations.
